title: Dead Water
subtitle: Thirty Days in Haskett County

listing.title: Dead Water 🧟
listing.blurb: The dead get up during the Ferry Days festival in a Missouri river town, and the Guard pulls out on day three. Thirty days of scavenging, barter and hard choices against the dead and against the grain co-op that has learned to steer them. Levels 1–6.

synopsis: Corbin's Ferry is a river town of forty-eight hundred people on the north bank of the Tamarack River in Haskett County, Missouri: one steel truss bridge, one grain elevator you can see from nine miles off, a lock and dam two miles downstream, and a Ferry Days festival every third weekend in September. This year, on the Saturday of Ferry Days, the dead start getting up. Nobody in Haskett County ever learns why, and the campaign never tells them. What it tells them instead, one hard lesson at a time, is how it works: a bite kills you, slowly and for certain; anyone who dies of anything comes back; and gunfire brings the dead from half a mile in every direction. The National Guard holds the Route 9 bridge for two days and then leaves. The phones die on day five and the power on day six. By the second week the people who are still alive have sorted themselves into holdouts: a hardware store on Front Street, a Mennonite farm community out on Prairie Hill, a church camp at Dutch Hollow, and the Haskett Farmers Co-op, which holds the elevator, the bridge, forty thousand gallons of diesel and one point eight million bushels of grain. The Co-op's general manager, Colleen Marsh, is a retired Army logistics officer who has done the arithmetic on how many people the county can feed, and she has decided who those people are. She has also discovered something nobody else has: the dead follow sound, and a tornado siren bolted to a grain truck can walk a horde anywhere you like. The player characters are survivors of Day One who end up holding Kettering Hardware & Feed. Over four scenarios and roughly thirty days they get out of town alive, cross the river to the regional hospital for medicine, uncover what the Co-op does to holdouts that refuse its tithe, and face the river herd — thousands of dead walking down the valley from the cities upstream — while Colleen Marsh tries to ring that herd straight through Corbin's Ferry. The dead are a weather system: relentless, predictable, survivable with care. The living are the campaign's real antagonist, because they think.
hook: It is the Saturday of Ferry Days, a warm one, the last of the summer. Front Street is closed to cars from the levee to the courthouse annex; there is a funnel-cake trailer, a fire-department dunk tank, a bluegrass band on a flatbed stage, and four hundred people who have mostly known each other since kindergarten. At about twenty past four a towboat called the Ruth Ellen noses into the public landing without signalling, too fast, and grinds against the boat ramp, and nobody comes out of the wheelhouse. Two volunteer firemen go aboard. One of them comes back down the gangway holding his forearm and laughing about it, saying the deckhand bit him, the deckhand is out of his mind on something, call the sheriff. Twenty minutes later the fireman is sitting in the first-aid tent beside the Lions Club booth, grey and sweating. An hour after that he has stopped breathing, and the nurse working the tent is pulling the curtain shut, and the fireman sits up. You are on Front Street when the screaming starts. Some of you came for the festival, some of you work here, one of you was in the first-aid tent. The band has stopped. The sheriff's cruiser that was parked at the barricade is empty with its door open. You can hear sirens over the river in Haskett, more than one, and you can see people running down Front Street toward you who are not running away from anything — they are running at you. The only building on the block with a steel door is Kettering Hardware & Feed.

setting.name: Haskett County, Missouri
setting.description: A rural county in the Missouri interior, cut east to west by the Tamarack River on its way to the Mississippi. Corbin's Ferry sits on the north bank: a grid of brick downtown blocks along Front Street and the levee, a water tower, a Dollar General, three churches, a feed store, a high school whose football field is the flattest open ground for miles, and KHCF 1340 AM, the county's one radio station, broadcasting from a cinder-block building under its own tower on the bluff. The two-lane Route 9 truss bridge crosses south to Harmon Siding, where the rail spur, the co-op fuel depot and the Haskett Farmers Co-op grain elevator stand — a white concrete tower a hundred and forty feet high that is the tallest thing in the county and can be seen from everywhere in it. Eight miles further south is the county seat, Haskett (pop. 11,000), and St. Agnes Regional Medical Center, the only hospital in three counties. Two miles downstream of Corbin's Ferry is Lock and Dam No. 14, a 1930s Army Corps structure with a lock wall a person can walk across. West is farmland, bottomland timber and gravel county roads: the Mennonite community on Prairie Hill, the Lutheran church camp at Dutch Hollow, and the flooded limestone quarry at Sullivan Ridge. It is late September and it has been the driest summer in thirty years: the Tamarack is at record low water, and below the dam the river breaks into sandbars a person can wade between.
setting.atmosphere: Network-television horror, not splatter. The dead are frightening because of what they used to be — the man who ran the Lions Club booth, the girl from the Dollar General register — and because they never stop coming, not because the camera lingers on wounds. Describe sound before sight: the shuffle on gravel, the moan that carries over water, the way a dog barks itself hoarse three farms away. Describe the ordinary world going off one system at a time: the phones, the radio, the power, the last news anchor. Daylight is precious and the nights are long and quiet and full of small noises. The county is beautiful in the way it always was — the river at sunset, the soybeans going gold, the elevator white against the sky — and that beauty is part of the horror. The tone is grief and stubbornness more than despair: people bury their dead when they can, share what they have when they can afford to, and argue about whether they can afford to. There is no cure, no secret lab, no military rescue at the end, and no explanation. There is the county, and the people still in it, and what they decide to be.

regions.name: Corbin's Ferry (north bank)
regions.description: The party's home ground. Front Street and the levee, the public landing and boat ramp, the Landing Bar, Kettering Hardware & Feed (brick, two storeys, steel back door, loading dock, roof hatch), the police department and its two-cell jail, the high school, the Dollar General out on the highway, and KHCF 1340 AM on the bluff. On Day One about two hundred townspeople turn in the first six hours; by the end of the first week perhaps two hundred living people are left in town, scattered in houses, the Methodist church and the school gym. Downtown is a maze of alleys, back stairs and flat tar roofs: a careful party can cross six blocks without touching the street.

regions.name: Harmon Siding and the Route 9 Bridge
regions.description: The south end of the bridge, and the Co-op's fortress. The Haskett Farmers Co-op elevator and its bins, the rail spur with a stranded string of forty grain hoppers, the co-op fuel depot (40,000 gallons of diesel and gasoline in above-ground tanks), the anhydrous ammonia tanks, the scale house and the Co-op office. After Day Four the Co-op holds the bridge with a checkpoint of grain trucks parked nose to tail and a deer stand welded on top of a combine. Everyone who crosses the river by road goes through Wade Pruitt's census table.

regions.name: Haskett and St. Agnes
regions.description: The county seat, eight miles south of the river: a courthouse square, a Walmart Supercenter that was looted bare by Day Three, the sheriff's office, and St. Agnes Regional Medical Center — four storeys, a helipad, a parking garage, and the county's entire supply of insulin, antibiotics and surgical equipment. Haskett had eleven thousand people and lost most of them in the first week, because the hospital was where the first bites were brought. It is the most dangerous place in the campaign that is not on fire.

regions.name: The West County: Prairie Hill, Dutch Hollow, Sullivan Ridge
regions.description: Gravel roads, fence lines, soybean fields and bottomland timber. The Mennonite farms on Prairie Hill — thirty families, horse-and-buggy-adjacent, with wells, root cellars, draft horses and a deep reluctance to shoot anyone — become the county's quiet second holdout. The Lutheran church camp at Dutch Hollow holds sixty townspeople until the night in week two when a horde comes out of nowhere. The flooded limestone quarry at Sullivan Ridge has one gated road in and sheer walls, which is exactly why the Co-op uses it.

regions.name: The River: Lock and Dam No. 14 and the Low Water
regions.description: The Tamarack runs slow and brown and, this year, shallow. Lock and Dam No. 14 holds a pool upstream deep enough for barges; below it, at record low water, the river braids into sandbars and gravel shoals that a determined walker — living or dead — can cross on foot. The dam has nine tainter gates operated from a control house on the lock wall, and a lockmaster, Bert Lindqvist, who has not left his post. The towboat Mary Delaine is tied up in the lock approach with two barges of fertilizer and a full fuel bunker. The river is the only way across the county that the Co-op does not control.

campaignRules.name: Infection: The Bite Is Fixed
campaignRules.description: Only a zombie's BITE infects. Whatever a zombie statblock lists, in this campaign its bite can only hit a creature it is grappling, or one that is prone or restrained; its other attacks (grabs, slams, claws) do damage but never infect. A bite that deals damage = Infected. Blood or fluid in the eyes or mouth (a GM-declared event, e.g. a Bloater bursting at point blank) calls for a DC 12 CON save; failure = Infected. Once Infected, THE OUTCOME IS FIXED: the character will die and rise. There is no cure, no immunity, no lucky natural 20, and the GM never invents one. What the dice decide is how long and how well the character lasts. Every 4 hours after the bite the character makes a DC 12 CON save; each FAILURE advances one stage (successes simply hold the stage): Stage 1 Fever — cannot regain HP from hit dice; Stage 2 Sick — poisoned condition; Stage 3 Failing — HP maximum halved, speed 15, Shaken; Stage 4 — the character dies, and rises 1d10 minutes later as a Zombie Runner (the bitten always come back fast). However well the saves go, a character who has not reached Stage 4 within 48 hours of the bite dies at that mark: that is the outer limit, and the GM says so. WHAT A MEDIC CAN DO: (1) AMPUTATION — only for a bite on a hand, forearm, foot or lower leg, and only within 1 minute (10 rounds) of the bite. It takes an action with a blade or saw and a DC 15 Medicine check (trauma kit or Field Medicine gives advantage). Success: the infection is stopped; the character takes 3d6 slashing, is Bleeding, and loses the limb permanently (GM and player agree the consequences). Failure: same damage and Bleeding and the limb is lost, but roll a d6 — on 1–3 the infection had already passed and proceeds normally. Bites to the torso, neck or head cannot be amputated. (2) MANAGEMENT — a course of antibiotics or a fever-reducer plus rest gives advantage on the next CON save; Field Medicine heals HP normally. (3) COMFORT — morphine or a sedative lets a Stage 3 character die asleep. WHAT A MEDIC CANNOT DO: cure it, slow it past 48 hours, or tell from the wound whether it will turn (it always does). PLAYER COURTESY: tell the player the rule the moment their character is bitten, in plain words. An infected character is played to the end by their player, and the player decides how it goes; give them a scene.

campaignRules.name: Everyone Rises
campaignRules.description: Every person who dies in Haskett County, of anything — bites, gunshots, heart attacks, a fall — rises as a Zombie Shambler 2d6 minutes after death, unless the brain is destroyed (an action against the body with any weapon, no roll) or the body is burned. The party does not know this at the start of the campaign; they learn it in ob-scenario-002, in the St. Agnes morgue. Until then, play it straight and let it surprise them once. After that it is a standing obligation the GM should remind them of: after every fight, someone has to make sure. This also means a dead PC rises. The GM should allow the dead PC's player to narrate the companion who takes care of it.

campaignRules.name: Horde Attention (Noise)
campaignRules.description: This campaign's teeth on the core gunplay Noise rule. The GM keeps an ATTENTION score for the current area (a few blocks in town, a farmstead, a floor of a building) and says it OUT LOUD whenever it changes — the players should always know where they stand. Each round in which anyone fires an unsuppressed gun: +1 (shotgun, magnum or rifle: +2; full auto, suppressive fire or an explosion: +3). Vehicle engine running nearby: +1 per 10 minutes. Breaking glass, a car alarm, screaming: +1 each. A siren, an air horn or the Co-op's Bell: +5 per round. Suppressed shots and melee: +0, unless a fight drags past 5 rounds (+1). Thresholds: ATTENTION 3 — 1d4 Zombie Shamblers arrive in 1d4 rounds. ATTENTION 6 — a Horde has turned toward the sound and arrives in 2d4 rounds outdoors (immediately, from the stairwells, indoors); add a Zombie Runner or two in town. ATTENTION 9 — everything within half a mile converges: two Hordes plus whatever is in the scenario, arriving over 1d4 minutes; the area is HOT and stays at 6 for the next 24 hours. Attention falls by 2 for every 10 minutes of real quiet and resets overnight unless the area is HOT. Indoors, the whole building hears a gunshot; outdoors, roughly half a mile does. The dead also follow light at night (a lit window or headlights on an open road: +1 per 10 minutes) and follow the living by sight. The point of the rule is a real choice every fight: the gun ends this fight faster and starts the next one.

campaignRules.name: Melee, Guns and the Dead
campaignRules.description: Melee is quiet, cheap and dangerous: it costs no ammunition and adds no Attention, but it puts you inside a zombie's reach, where a grab can become a bite. Guns are safe at range, loud, and finite. Zombies fight to 0 HP; a called shot to the head (−5, per the gunplay rules) is a critical hit, and a melee attacker who has advantage against a zombie may call the head for the same −5. Zombies are immune to being Shaken, Suppressed or frightened, ignore Intimidation, and cannot be talked to. A zombie that has a creature grappled must use its next attack on a Bite; breaking a grapple (Athletics or Acrobatics vs. the zombie's grapple DC) is the most important action in the game. Doors stop Shamblers (a closed door holds for ten rounds against one, two rounds against a Horde); barricades are Jury-Rig work. The dead do not open doors, climb ladders or swim with purpose, but they fall down stairs, wade, and pile up.

campaignRules.name: Ammunition Is What You Have
campaignRules.description: Every round of ammunition a character owns is a counted line on their sheet — 9mm rounds (24) — and that number INCLUDES whatever is loaded; the magazine size only says how many can be fired before a Reload. The GM deducts rounds with TrackResources 'use' once per exchange (single 1, burst 3, auto 10, suppressive 10) as the shots happen, never in a lump afterwards. Out is out. There is no resupply in this campaign except what is found in the scenarios, which list it in exact counts, and what is bartered. The calibres in the county are 9mm, .38 Special, .357, .22 LR, 12-gauge, 5.56mm and .308; ammunition does not interchange. A Tech can reload spent brass at the safehouse with a press and components (if the party finds them in ob-scenario-003): 10 rounds per hour, Mechanics DC 12, a failure ruins the batch.

campaignRules.name: Scarcity and Barter
campaignRules.description: Dollars are the campaign currency, and they rot. Days 1–4: cash works, at five times normal prices, and people still take a check out of habit. Days 5–10: some people take cash, nobody gives change, and fifty dollars buys what a single round of ammunition does. After Day 10: nobody takes money at all except the Co-op, which takes it as kindling. Real value lives in TRADE GOODS, and the GM should price anything worth having in them. Barter rates in the second week (the Co-op Market posts them on a chalkboard): 1 round of pistol ammunition = 1 day of food for one person; 1 rifle round or shotgun shell = 2 days of food; 1 gallon of gasoline or diesel = 5 pistol rounds; 1 course of antibiotics (10 days) = 50 pistol rounds; 1 vial of insulin = 30 pistol rounds; 1 working radio with batteries = 40 pistol rounds; a medkit = 25; a box of 9V/AA batteries = 10; a live chicken = 5; a pound of coffee = 8; a pack of cigarettes = 3. Prices move with events and the GM moves them. Write trade goods on the sheet as counted lines exactly like ammunition — Antibiotics (2 courses), Gasoline (5 gallons) — so they can be tracked with TrackResources. Rewards in scenarios list cash because cash is what lies around; tell the players what it is worth that week.

campaignRules.name: The Safehouse
campaignRules.description: Kettering Hardware & Feed on Front Street is the party's base from ob-scenario-001 onwards (they may move; the rule moves with them). The safehouse has three tracked numbers the GM keeps visible: SECURITY 0–5 (start 1: one steel door), SUPPLIES in person-days of food and water, and OCCUPANTS (party, companions and whoever they take in). A long rest regains everything ONLY in a place with Security 2+ and someone on watch; a long rest anywhere else is a short rest unless the GM rolls no interruption on a d6 roll of 4+ (on a 1, the dead arrive). Raising Security by 1 takes a day's work by three people plus materials and a Jury-Rig or Mechanics check (DC 10 for Security 2, then 12, 15, 18, 20): boarded windows, a roof watch, a generator, a cleared fire lane, a back gate. At Security 3+ a Horde that reaches the building does not get in on its own, but noise inside still counts for Attention. Each day costs one Supply per occupant; at zero, each occupant gains a level of exhaustion per day without food. Taking people in is the safehouse's whole moral economy: every mouth costs a Supply, every pair of hands is labour. The GM should make that a real decision, never a trick.

campaignRules.name: Shaken: Morale and Breaking Points
campaignRules.description: The core condition Shaken (disadvantage on WIS and CHA checks and saves until a short rest) is this campaign's morale track. A character makes a DC 12 WIS save or becomes Shaken when they: see someone they know turn or have to put them down; are bitten, or watch a companion be bitten; see a Horde in the open for the first time in a scenario; or do something they cannot square with themselves (GM and player agree). A Face's Rally ends Shaken as well as frightened. A long rest at a safehouse with Security 2+ ends it; a short rest only ends it if the character spends it talking to someone. BREAKING POINT: a character who becomes Shaken for the third time without a long rest between gains a lasting scar — the player writes a new flaw on the sheet, in their own words, and it stays. This is not a punishment. It is how the county marks people, and it should be played with the same seriousness as a lost limb.

campaignRules.name: The Living
campaignRules.description: Human enemies use the full gunplay rules and the shared adversary statblocks (Civilian, Street Thug, Gang Enforcer, Gang Boss, Beat Cop, Soldier (Infantry), Sniper, Mercenary, Guard Dog, Attack Dog). They take cover, aim, suppress, flank, retreat, surrender and remember. They know about Noise and use it: the Co-op will deliberately start shooting near a party to bring the dead down on them, and will happily fight at ATTENTION 6 from a rooftop. Unlike the dead, the living can be bargained with, lied to, frightened, shamed and split, and the campaign is built so that the smartest way through every Co-op problem is a conversation or a broadcast, not a gunfight. The Co-op's ordinary members are farmers, truck drivers, cashiers and their kids; most of them do not know what the Bell is for.

wildernessStarts.label: Front Street, Corbin's Ferry — Ferry Days

explorationRules: Run the campaign on a DAY COUNT and say it at the top of every session: Day 1 is the Saturday of Ferry Days. The world shuts down on a fixed schedule that the GM honours whatever the party does: Day 2 the Missouri National Guard sets up at the Route 9 bridge; Day 3 the Guard pulls out at dawn; Day 4 the Co-op takes the bridge; Day 5 the cell network goes; Day 6 the power grid goes (generators work, fuel matters); Day 9 the last national radio broadcast ends mid-sentence; Day 12 the Dutch Hollow camp falls; around Day 24 the river herd reaches the county. Travel by vehicle is fast and loud (+1 Attention per 10 minutes, and the roads are choked with abandoned cars: a Piloting DC 12 check per 5 miles or lose 20 minutes and gain Attention); travel on foot is quiet and slow (2 miles an hour cross-country, 3 on roads). Going anywhere costs daylight, and daylight matters: at night the dead are harder to see and lights draw them. Scavenging a building takes 30 minutes per floor and an Investigation or Perception check (DC 10 houses, 12 shops, 15 anywhere already picked over); the GM should give real, counted finds on a success — '9mm rounds (11)', 'Canned food (6 person-days)' — and a complication on a failure (a Shambler in a closet, a noise, someone else's claim). Most of all, the county should feel like a place that keeps happening when the party is not looking: other survivors move, the Co-op expands, houses get emptied, and the dead drift with the wind and the sound.
